utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Cavoski. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Cavoski.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, could you please tell us your full name, surname, father's name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Kosta Cavoski. I was born in Banatsko Novo Selo on the 26th of October, 1941. My father's name is Savo, and my mother's name is Vera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation and I also ask you to pay attention to your screen, and then only when the translation is finished then we can continue. I'm not going to ask you to talk about your works; that would take a long time. But I would like to start from the top and to say that other than the fact that you are a member of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences, could you please tell us what your qualifications are and your career path?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I came to the faculty -- I graduated from the faculty of law in Belgrade in 1964. For a while I was professionally involved in politics as part of the student and the youth organisations. I was the international vice-president of the association of students of Yugoslavia. Then I decided to work in research and so I did my masters and the thesis was called: The role of the American Supreme Court in shaping American federalism, which qualified me as a historian familiar with American constitutional history. Then I began to work as a teaching associate at the faculty, and then I had my doctorate in the idea of freedom and democracy or the possibility of freedom and democracy. I was an associate lecturer until 1971. Then I was thrown out because the year before that I was convicted for the delict of opinion because of a work which was published in the magazine of "Glediste" under the title of the value of Yugoslav law. And for that offence I was sentenced to a jail sentence of five months conditionally over a period of two years, and that was the reason why I was thrown out of the university, and for two years I was unemployed. I worked on translations and, among other things, I translated two treaties on the government by John Locke. Also a famous work by the patriarch written by Firmer [phoen], an English writer from the 16th century, who talked about the divine role of kings. And then only at 1978 I began to work at the institute for management law where I worked for ten years, then I worked at the institute for philosophy and theory -- I'm sorry, thank you. And then on the 1st of January, 1991, again I was employed as a full-time professor at the faculty of law in Belgrade, where I completed and did my career at the age of 68 as a tenured professor, of course, and now I'm retired. In the meantime, in 2003, I was -- I became a member of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences. This is my career in brief. If necessary, I can clarify certain things or add some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Even though the -- your CV is very long, I would just like you to tell us some of the most important things that were published in your profession, and could you please tell us something about any specialised fields that you particularly focused on during your career?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Because I had problems when I testified in the case of Stanislav Galic because there I just summarised by bibliography, this time I asked my colleagues in the Serbian academy of arts and sciences to draft a proper bibliography, according to their standards. So all the books are listed there, not only by title but also with a short summary, so you can see what the content is. My first book was "Philosophy of Open Society, Political De-liberalism" by Karl Popper --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have this bibliography.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, while I was younger I did not do that so frequently, but now that I am older I'm working more and more so that I published some 37 books. The ones that I can emphasize is the book: "The Possibility of Freedom in Democracy," or, for example, the book: "Constitutionality and Federalism, Court Monitoring of Constitutionality in Anglo-Saxon States," thinking of the United States, Canada, and Australia. We're talking about the constitutional oversight -- judicial review of constitutional matters. Then many other books followed; for example, "Party Multi-Pluralism or Monism..." published in English which I published together with Vojislav Kostunica, who is a bit younger than I am. And after the fall of Milosevic he was first the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and then after that the president or the prime minister, Serbian prime minister. What is a little bit unusual for lawyers, people in the legal professional, which is my profession is that I also studied Aeschylus, who is an old ancient Greek writer of tragedies and perhaps one of the greatest poets. I translated his trilogy called Oresteia, where I showed through interpreting his verses what his position was on absolute and modified justice. Also an unusual thing is that I was also studying political and legal philosophy. I have a study on John Locke. He is one of the first great liberals of the 17th century in England. And then I have a large monograph which I believe is original. It's a study on Machiavelli.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is too much interference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Probably, Doctor, you are speaking a bit too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will slow down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- from what you talked about Machiavelli.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After Machiavelli I also published a large number of books, thanks to which I was able to summarise my reviews and studies and publish them as some kind of an annal or review. I was very interested in legal and political conditions in the former Yugoslavia, especially in the period before the dissolution of that state, the situation in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, Montenegro, Serbia, and so on and so forth. So I was one of the best-known political analysts of that time. And because of that and because of this large number of books, and also as the Prosecutor noted in the Galic case, he said that I also wrote expert analysis on the work of The Hague Tribunal or the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Two of those studies were published in English also. The first dealt with the case of General Djordje Djukic, who died without seeing the trial to its completion. The second is the case of President Radovan Karadzic. At the time when there were just two indictments which were later amended, this was published twice in English. The second edition also contained some accompanying documents. I think for now this is sufficient and of course, if required, I can speak more about my works.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Cavoski. And specially I thank you for slowing down your pace because then it could all be recorded in the transcript. As you said yourself, you know, you are aware of what I am charged with. And in the third final indictment I am charged with -- for my alleged participation in a comprehensive joint criminal enterprise and three subsequent criminal enterprises. The main goal of these criminal enterprises are the lasting removal of Muslims and Croats from the territories to which the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina lay claim, and then the indictment also states that the Prosecutor does not believe that I committed the crimes myself physically but that my responsibility lies pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal for participation in the joint criminal enterprise. These allegations mostly are based on reports of two experts of the Prosecution: Robert Donia and Patrick Treanor. And so you are asked to study these reports and to submit your own report about whether their reports are accurate, what is stated in them, whether that is accurate. And now I would like to ask you -- well, we do have your report, it's a little bit summarised. It's a shorter version of the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, while I've had occasion in the past to object to needless commentary by the accused, I considered that this might be a fairly and clumsy long-winded attempt to move into the question but it contained commentary that is both impermissible and erroneous. For example, these allegations mostly are based on reports, it's neither the accused's province to offer such commentary nor, obviously, is that a correct submission. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Otherwise it is of leading nature as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's very true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, I do understand. But I don't wish to -- well, I want to say what we are asking Professor Cavoski to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Cavoski, could you briefly tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe that's a perfect opportunity to say it's not for Mr. Karadzic to say what Mr. Cavoski was asked to do. He is to ask the witness and to find out what the witness's position is in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what's the problem with the accused asking the witness what he has been tasked to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That -- I have no problem with that, Mr. President. It's just that Mr. Karadzic was excusing what happened before by saying essentially he wants to say what he was asked to do. That's been the problem throughout. It's Dr. Karadzic who wants to tell the witness what his evidence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it by now Mr. Karadzic has understood it. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, line 9, page 7, this is precisely what I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Cavoski, could you please tell us what it was that the Defence asked you to do?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I was asked to carefully review and study the reports of two experts: One is Dr. Robert Donia and the other is Dr. Patrick Treanor. I did that and, as is usual in studies of this kind, I attempted to discover their material errors, inconsistencies, omissions of key facts, and periodical malicious things that cropped up in the reports. And thereby I tried to bring into question their credibility and veracity. That is the nature of my report. By its nature, it's an analytical report. I pointed, first of all, to the omissions in those reports in order to show that the reports cannot be accepted as such in their entirety. I can cite a number of examples where the errors are evident. On page 6 I mentioned a quotation from Robert Donia where he says -- it's on page 52, obvious errors, under 1, page 52 where it says: [In English] "... MUP officers of Serb nationality dressed in the blue uniforms ...," and so on. [Interpretation] So as you can see he claims that the Serbian policemen differed from others by their blue uniforms. And on this fact that they wore blue uniforms he draws the conclusion that these were Serbian policemen. I am sufficiently old and I have relatively good memory and I know for sure that all policemen in the former Yugoslavia from Jesenica to Djevdjelija used to wear blue uniforms. Therefore, a blue uniform was not a hallmark of a Serb policeman but of any policeman. And it's obvious that this is a material error if not malevolence. On page 7 which is -- it says here page 79, a person is mentioned, and the name of this person is - pay attention to the name - Rizo Selmanagic, and then it says a Serb veteran of the Second World War. All right. I apologise. Thank you. So it is said of Rizo Selmanagic that he was a Serb veteran from the Second World War. Those of us who live in the territory of the former Yugoslavia know well what names mean. On the basis of names we're able to recognise the ethnicity of a person. For example, my name is Serbian, my first name is Serbian, but the last name not quite. That's why people sometimes wonder what my ethnicity is. I am a Serb, but I don't have a typical Serbian last name. However, someone who is called Rizo Selmanagic cannot be anything else but a Muslim. There were of courses Muslims who declared themselves as Serbs. For example, Alija Izetbegovic in the first census that was conducted declared himself a Serb because there were only three possibilities, to declare himself a Serb, a Croat, or as a non-aligned. There was no possibility to declare himself as a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please focus on certain areas. Could you tell us how in these reports the period before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the period of the Yugoslav crisis is depicted. How did they understand it and how did they describe it? Can we just hear that from you briefly? Because we have your report and I hope it will be admitted. What we do not have is your assessment. How did they understand this, and how did they describe it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I thank you for the interruption and please interrupt me every time, President Karadzic, whenever you believe that I am too extensive in my statement because this is probably not necessary for the expert testimony. My assessment is that the authors of both reports, Dr. Donia, who makes many more errors, and Patrick Treanor, in whose report I found only three insignificant material reports [as interpreted], by my judgement, mostly described in a very inadequate manner the circumstances in the former Yugoslavia on the eve of its breakup. A constitutional question arose at the time, whether Yugoslavia could be broken up or not and whether such an act would be constitutional or anti-constitutional. Both authors glossed over this significant issue, and with great sympathies, I have to say, mentioned the acts of the secessionists. First of all, the Slovenian and then the Croatian governments and eventually those committed by the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can understand that someone may believe that Yugoslavia needed to be broken up, but this had to be analysed in the context of whether that was allowed from the point of view of the constitution that was then in force or not. Both authors seemed to skip this fact, Donia with the justification that he did not deal with constitutional law even though he, himself, referred to the decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which denied the constitutionality of a Serbian institution, the National Council. And Patrick Treanor also did not deal with this issue. In my view, this is something that is lacking and it is significant because there was no constitutional basis for breaking up Yugoslavia. Also, they make wrong assessments of the role of the Yugoslav People's Army. The Yugoslav People's Army had the constitutional duty to protect and defend the territorial integrity of the former Yugoslavia. The fact that it failed to do so was its big weakness that will be judged by history and the peoples who were the victims. But it had to do that. Both Donia and Patrick Treanor, with regard to the role of the JNA, very often described that as if it defended only the Serb interests, the interests of the Serbian people, rather than the interests of all nations and nationalities that made up the then-Yugoslavia. For a long time there were six units, both provinces, Serbia and Montenegro, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia, which were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia. The only ones that opposed were Slovenia and Croatia. These two authors failed to note that. Then the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia made dozens and dozens of decisions which denied the constitutionality even of some constitutional laws of Slovenia and Croatia, then their regular laws and sub-laws. None of these decisions is mentioned in these reports, even though they do refer to a decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In my view, these were great shortcomings. And Dr. Karadzic asked me about their assessment and review of the circumstances and situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, 1991, before the breakup of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the former Yugoslavia which had already been broken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Of course I will ask you that. Can you please tell the Chamber what was actually happening before the breakout of the war in Bosnia as opposed to the way this is depicted in the two reports.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As I seriously study history, I claim that the real truth will only be discovered in about 30 years, once that all secret intelligence, diplomatic, and other archives of the USA, the UK, Germany, and other important states are open. What can be said on the basis of the materials that are available at the moment is that for quite a long time both the USA and the leading European powers were in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia within its borders. And then at one point, perhaps under the influence of Germany, there was a change and the conclusion which was adopted was that the so-called Versailles Yugoslavia needed to be broken up, the Yugoslavia which was created by the peace treaty of Versailles, and the borders of which were established on the basis of the agreement signed at the Trianon with the neighbouring countries and so on. At that moment the foreign powers began to support the secession of Slovenia and Croatia, and then later on Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. So under such circumstances it was necessary to preserve first the then-Yugoslavia and then also Bosnia and Herzegovina at any cost. I was following the circumstances very closely because in addition to my scholarly work I was involved in politics throughout my career and I wrote articles and books simultaneously as the events were developing. You can see that from my bibliography what I was assessing. In my view the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina actually pursued three policies. One was primary or first rate, the other one was secondary, and they had a tertiary. The primary policy was the preservation of the integrity of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the preservation of Yugoslavia. So the preservation of Yugoslavia, that is to say Bosnia-Herzegovina as an integral part of Yugoslavia, all of Yugoslavia. At the moment when it was assessed that this would no longer be possible, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, led by the Serb Democratic Party, tried to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina within the so-called Rump Yugoslavia as we may call it, the Rump Yugoslavia. What was important about this was an agreement that was very important and had long-term consequences and which Adil Zulfikarpasic had made with Slobodan Milosevic and which preceded the so-called Cutileiro Plan. I personally knew this Adil Zulfikarpasic. I socialised with him since around 1986 when I returned from the United States. He was a very reasonable man and he concluded that the Muslims were living together with the Serbs in 103 Bosnian municipalities and in a much smaller number of municipalities together with Croats, and that it was most important that they should keep friendly relations with the Serbs. He claimed publicly that by authority, though a verbal one, of Alija Izetbegovic he had arrived in Belgrade and concluded the agreement which implied that Bosnia would remain a part of either Yugoslavia or the Rump Yugoslavia. The agreement was concluded and signed and publicly presented, but unfortunately Alija Izetbegovic later on said he wanted to have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you just to clarify this for us. Did you know how I reacted, what I agreed with Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic, and did the Serbs on their part give up some of their plans for the sake of preserving Bosnia within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: President Karadzic, of course I cannot remember every single detail, but I think that the Serbian Democratic Party abandoned its idea about regionalisation which had already been implemented and which was in accordance with the constitution and the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You were willing to give it up on condition that this plan was adopted. So both Filipovic and Adil Zulfikarpasic had left the Party of Democratic Action and formed their own party with a Bosniak name and negotiated. This was done by Adil Zulfikarpasic. The Serbs led by the Serbian Democratic Party really made a big concession to the Muslims by doing this in the hope that it was possible to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina and peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was especially important. Because in our Balkan region every inter-ethnic conflict sooner or later leads to a fratricide and sometimes even civil war. So the Serbian Democratic Party made this concession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please continue about item 2.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, another big opportunity to preserve peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Cutileiro Plan. He acted on the orders of the European Union. He was a Portuguese diplomat. On several occasions representatives of all three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina met; that is to say they were represented by Alija Izetbegovic, Mate Boban, and Dr. Radovan Karadzic. The plan had almost been agreed on. The principles had been accepted and signed, and these were basically the constitutional principles which implied the formation of three, we would say, constitutional or constitutive units. Today the word "entity" is more often used, but this would -- these would actually be confederal units or entities of Bosnia as an overall Federation. At first they did not have to, at least that was not envisaged, they did not have to be completely linked territorially. It was supposed that the municipalities with majority Muslim population would be part of the Muslim entity; others which had Serbian majority of the population would be in the Serbian entity; and likewise with the Croatian municipalities. But there were some disputed municipalities and arbitration of European Union was envisaged. The number of those disputed municipalities was not great and the commission had been set up which was supposed to resolve the issue. And this had almost been successfully completed, and then something unexpected happened, namely, the US ambassador, Warren Zimme rmann, who served in Belgrade arrived and talked to Alija Izetbegovic. The letter complained to him that, well, he had to sign this agreement with representatives of the Serbs and the Croats which he and the Muslims did not really find to be completely in their favour, to which as the media reports then said Zimmermann responded: And why would you have to do this? And so he drew a conclusion from that that the United States were not forcing the Bosnia-Herzegovina Muslims to do this. And then Alija Izetbegovic, in an act which was most heretical, withdrew his signature from the document where he had already placed his initials. I say he only initialled it because that was the preliminary form of the agreement. When I was a witness in the Stanislav Galic case, the Prosecutor read out to me an interview with Warren Zimmermann from much later on in which he claims things did not develop in this way. And how did they develop? This is something that the diplomatic archives will uncover in 25 or 30 years once it is available to curious scientists, scholars and journalists. We were convinced because that was the way it was described in the media at the time and Izetbegovic also told many people about this, that that was actually a dialogue that he had with Warren Zimmermann. So as you can see, and as I have written and published, this withdrawal of signature from the Cutileiro Plan which was treacherous was, as the lawyers would say, casus belli, the cause of war, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Izetbegovic was in a way aware of it. Because in 1943 -- in 1993, rather, he stated, I think it's somewhere in my report, I'm not sure which page that is on, that he more or less knew that if he had to choose between peace and the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he chose the latter. And of course the latter resulted in the civil war. However, the Tribunal is more interested in the consequence, whereas historians are more interested in responsibility. I as a historian must say that those are responsible for this war who refused to accept the Cutileiro Plan who, to my mind and in many people's opinions, was fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you mean the Tribunal or any court on page 16, line 10, as it was recorded? Or did you mean both? I'm referring to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: You mean here in front of me? I meant the International Criminal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we deny Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence in the context of the Cutileiro Plan? Did we refuse that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That solution was the least acceptable solution for the Serbs, but still acceptable. The most favourable variant would have been the preservation of Yugoslavia. Number two would have been what Adil Zulfikarpasic had proposed, namely, for BH to remain in the framework of a truncated Yugoslavia. And only -- the third solution that was very hard to accept for the Serbs was for Bosnia to become independent; namely, that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina be separated from the Serbs in Serbia and live in two different countries. But to preserve the peace or as we say sometimes to keep Bosnia peaceful, Bosnia was to be structured as a loose federation or confederation of three ethnic entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Cavoski, the model put forward by the European Union through Ambassador Cutileiro, was it something new or were you aware of similar examples in Europe, I mean this sort of structural type in another European country?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I have dealt with the matter of federalism for a long time, and Yugoslavia was a federation as well. Belgium, for example, which adopted its first constitution in 1835 or was it 33? I'm not sure. And the first Serbian constitution took that one as a model. Under that constitution Belgium was a unitary state, whereas nowadays it is a very loose confederation. The European Union wasn't much in favour of that but the Flemings wanted it. And the only thing keeping Belgium together is the city of Brussels which is on Flemish territory but has a Francophone majority. Europe does not support Scottish secession from England and the Scots were given to understand that if they decide to leave Great Britain - and I believe that they became part of Great Britain in 1701 - in that case they would have to wait for a number of years until they joined the European Union. This doesn't apply to Wales because the Welsh are not considering that. However, it does apply to Basque and Catalonia. These are two parts of Spain in which different languages from Spanish are spoken. The Basques speak a language which is unrelated to any other European language, whereas the Catalan was also developed from vulgar Latin. Then in Italy there is the idea of Padania which is the entire north of Italy as a separate state which would be economically more prosperous. And then there could also be the question of the secession of Sardinia and Sicily, because in Sardinia a special dialect is spoken which is actually Catalan. Sicily is a complex matter because it was formerly part of Magna Graecia, that is it belonged to the Greek civilisation. And then it was part of the Roman Empire and after that for a number of centuries the Arabs were present. And this population is very mixed and have a special mentality. When Italy was defeated, the Sicilians actually wanted to join the United States of America as the 49th state, I think. This problem could also arise in Transylvania, where there are many more Hungarians than in Serbia, and they live in a homogenous territory where they have been present for centuries. There are also very many Hungarians in the south of Slovakia that could also secede. Things are not at all easy in Europe. They're not as simple as they may look. The European Union never supported secession except in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You have noticed that these constituent units didn't have to be territorially contiguous. To what extent is that similar to the Swiss model where there are cantons which are established on a linguistic basis but are not territorially contiguous?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Switzerland is a unique federation, the only federation in the world which is not modelled after America - that's where all authors agree - whereas our federation and the Soviet federation was also modelled after the American one. Initially they only had three cantons which united, and then the number of cantons increased. But what determined the fate of Switzerland was the war of the seventh year in 1807. That was a war between the cantons, and the Bern canton was able to defeat the Catholics and make sure that Switzerland remain an entity. There was also the separation of a canton from another, the canton Jura, because they had a different religion. But the Swiss live in peace now. The principle is the following: Apart from the cantons which have different criminal codes, only the civil code is the same for all of Switzerland. They have four ethnic groups: The Germans who are mostly Protestants which is very important; then the French who are also Protestants; then there are Italians; and there's a small group of a few ten thousand who speak a language that developed from vulgar Latin, but they are also entitled to speak their own language in the assembly. So there are four ethnic entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us return to the Cutileiro Plan and the Lisbon Agreement. Did you notice or can it be found that in that agreement which the Serbs accepted and remained faithful to it, there are any grounds for persecution and the expulsion of population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Did you notice or can it be found in that agreement which the Serbs accepted and remained faithful to it...," again I object to the accused testifying and feeding information to witnesses -- or purporting to testify in those comments and thus feeding information to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, but that's what Professor Cavoski's report says. These are his very words, that the Serbs remained faithful to that agreement until the end, and this Bench knows that we never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the witness's previous answer, the Chamber has no difficulty with allowing the question. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the question? Does that agreement contain any foundation that would make possible or even oblige anybody to commit crimes, genocide, or even transfer population? Or did you know what my position and the Serbian position was with regard to exchange of population, let alone with regard to destruction, persecution, and extermination?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: President Karadzic, you don't have to tell me what is contained in that agreement because I know it very well. I followed the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina very closely and I collected documents. Occasionally I wrote about it, and at least once and maybe more often I wrote about the Cutileiro Plan as well. That's part of my bibliography. That plan does not envisage any re-settlement of population, let alone anything worse than that. It was supposed that everybody would stay where they were living, the places where the Serbian majority would be part of the Serbian entity; those in the Muslim majority part of Muslim entity, and so on. And then there was the issue of contentious municipalities. That was to be resolved. And those were such municipalities where one ethnicity had only a relative majority not an absolute one. When -- it has to do with the drawing of borders of the Croatian Banovina in 1939 which you know very well. Re-settlement of population was not envisaged, let alone violent acts or even genocide. Nothing of this kind was mentioned, and I'm surprised that anybody may make such inferences. It was a usual agreement which envisaged the federalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you characterise the acceptability of Mr. Izetbegovic's giving up on the agreement and opting for independence? What were our option in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could we -- were we able to accept this ruse?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: President Karadzic, that is a political question because one thing is what was written about and what was discussed, whereas another matter is the political usefulness. You were the leader of a people and you took decisions that you thought were in the best Serbian interest. If you're asking me for my personal opinion, I favoured the use of the Yugoslav People's Army, that was my personal attitude, my personal opinion, not yours, because we -- I thought that the country must be defended and that's what the army is for. But my personal opinion is irrelevant here and these proceedings. Izetbegovic, however, had to know that his refusal of the Cutileiro Plan would result in war. And this horrible consequence was something that he accepted in advance by refusing the Cutileiro Plan. And his travels to Libya several times and then to Turkey where he offended the Turks because he refused to bow at the mausoleum of Ataturk, but he did get some kind of support from Iran, for example. How much he exactly got, I don't know, but it was probably significant, a significant amount. But he will have to face the judgement of history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly in one sentence why Izetbegovic refused to pay honours to Ataturk at his mausoleum?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Izetbegovic personally and his son would come to see me sometimes while I was living on Maksim Gorki Street. He was imprisoned for -- because he was a dissenter. And he was a true believer in -- Muslim believer. Kemal Ataturk was in favour of a secular Turkey, not something few people know. He abolished the caliphate and all the Muslim priests were marginalised. And Izetbegovic condemned Ataturk's secularism and that's why he refused to bow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do the attempts to preserve peace and the acceptance of the Lisbon Agreement and Cutileiro Plan characterise these two expert reports that you studied and that were submitted here to this Court as evidence?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I study history a lot and recently I have been looking into antique ancient historians such as Thucydides, Xenophon, Tacitus, Suetonius, and in particular, Polybius, and some of them I quoted. And this is what is very important when we're talking about historians. It's not just important for them to refer to facts, to things that really occurred. What is important is in the sea of facts to discover those that are most important in order to explain the causes of certain events. And, you see, historian Robert Donia, he's a professor, a historian, he did not do that. He had to have wanted to find the crucial facts that resulted in the outbreak of war, not only in the former Yugoslavia but in particular in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These facts would be secession -- the secession of the Croatian and the Slovenian government, that would be a cause of war in the former Yugoslavia, as well as the attempt to set up an independent and sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina which would be majority Muslim on the ruins of former Yugoslavia. And you would reach the facts by rejecting the historical agreement between Zulfikarpasic and Milosevic and then by rejecting the Cutileiro Plan. How come Robert Donia never asked himself what casus belli was on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a key issue. Anybody studying seriously history would have had to have dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Cavoski, could you please tell us if there are any international legal duties or documents that would oblige us to accept a violent unilateral, unconstitutional, and disagreed secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to accept the rule of a minority Muslim population over a majority Christian one?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I dealt with federalism and secession as well as valid international law, and I must say that during the past 20 years some crucial changes have taken place. A former UN Secretary-General said that there was no question of breaking up a member of the United Nations, it was out of the question. So the possibility was not permitted for any member of the UN to be disbanded from outside or from the inside as a state. So the right of secession or independence was exclusively applied to former colonial peoples and to their liberation from the colonial domination of European powers. There is no federation in the world except the former Soviet Union which permitted secession. In the United States - this was controversial - two major writers, Taylor and Calhoun [phoen] did look at that possibility. And since it could not be resolved legally, this question was resolved in battle by the defeat of the southern states in 1865. And after that the US court - and I quoted that case, Texas versus White - was of the opinion that the American Union was indestructible consisting of indestructible member states. No attempts succeeded at secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, we don't have a lot of time so are you able to tell us --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will make breaks, thank you, and we will speak slower. Can you please tell us how Serbian agreements to preserve the peace and to preserve the unity of Bosnia and Herzegovina were presented in these reports by the experts that was submitted by these courts, also the preservation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, President Karadzic, they were not even dealt with. They were not presented. They did not feel the need to state that Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina led by the Serbian Democratic Party were prepared to make major concessions, to give up the constitutional framework of the former Yugoslavia, to give up the links, territorial and state links with Serbs in Serbia, just in order to preserve the peace. So this is not talked about in any way in these reports. Whenever needed - and I mention this in a number of places - there was a malicious attempt to show that the Yugoslav People's Army allegedly acted exclusively in the interests of the Serbs, which I think was absolutely wrong, wrongly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell us how these reports presented the chain of events and Serbian conduct after armed conflict broke out and how were the measures for the self-organisation and self-protection or the conduct of the Serbian party, how were they presented in this report or these reports, the appearance of staffs and all the other measures that the Serbian people in those circumstances, a completely newly occurring situation, carried out?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to talk about something that is frequently mentioned, and that is the Crisis Staff, the term "kriza," "crisis," which in old Greek means the moment of taking a decision. It was used a lot in the 1980s in Yugoslavia because socialism was in crisis, then the ruling party was in crisis, and then there were these so-called crisologists who dealt with that. Former Yugoslavia as well as former Bosnia-Herzegovina had laws on All People's Defence and social self-protection, and these laws provided for specific measures in the event of any danger of a conflict, internal uprisings, or in the event of an external attack. The formation of Crisis Staffs in that opinion was a legitimate, legal measure, which was taken in the event of the worst possible scenario happening. So when you foresee the possibility of a conflict breaking out, then you need to take measures, precautionary measures. So these Crisis Staffs were a preparatory measure in the event that the worst things came to pass. I wanted to just refresh everybody's memory and talk about two great thinkers in the field of political philosophy - these are Thomas Hobbes and John Locke - who had the idea of a natural state of affairs. A natural state is the state that precedes the establishment of a state or occurs after the breakup of a state so that a natural state would also be a state of civil war, just like a natural state could be a presentation of actual international affairs in times of conflicts and disagreements. So if somebody feels that a state is going to fall apart and that the existing government would not be able to protect its citizens, would not be able to protect -- vouch for their safety and for their property, then they allow for the possibility for them to take measures of precaution, measures of self-organising, in the event that such circumstances should occur bordering on the natural state of affairs in the Hobbesian sense of that idea. So I think that the Serbian side -- not just the Serbian side, though, both the Muslim and the Croatian side also did that, all three sides established Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was most prominent headed by the seventh member of the Presidency, Ejup Ganic, who was elected as an alleged Yugoslav-oriented person even though he was a Muslim by ethnicity. He was the head of that Crisis Staff and he tried in that way to bypass the powers of the two Serbian representatives: Professor Biljana Plavsic and Professor Nikola Koljevic. So that was the reason why this Crisis Staff later was abolished. The Croats also set up Crisis Staffs, the Muslims as well, and of course the Serbs did too. And in my view, this was not only in line with the valid laws on All People's Defence and civilian self-protection, but it was a precautionary measure in the event of the worst scenario occurring, which it actually did occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this process -- in this case the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbs in Bosnia are condemned the most for drafting a paper, instructions in the event of extraordinary circumstances which is popularly abbreviated to Variant A and B because those were the options presented in the paper. I'm not going to go into those who drafted this paper. All I want to ask you is this: Are you familiar with that paper and are you able to tell us if that paper is to blame for causing the crisis and does the crisis stem from that paper and is it legal in terms of the Yugoslav laws then in force?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: The paper as such cannot cause anything without the people who would act pursuant to things stated in the paper. I did have those instructions in my hands. I carefully studied it, both Variant A and B, its two parts, and I believe that it was in line with the then-valid laws on All People's Defence and social self-protection. Plan A provided for the formation of Crisis Staffs in those municipalities in which the Serbs were in a majority and they -- the mayor would be from the ranks of the Serbs because that's how they were elected, according to the majority population. Option B provided for the municipalities where the Serbs were in a minority to organise special Crisis Staffs which would encompass those settlements and villages where the Serbs were in a majority and in the town itself where they constituted a minority in the event that the safety and property was seriously endangered. This was a measure - how shall I put it? - of a precautionary nature in anticipation of anything that could possibly happen, which necessarily need not have happened, but regretfully had Cutileiro's plan been accepted, war could have been avoided, so that this instruction about the activities of the Crisis Staff would not have been implemented at all in that case. However, in my view, those who drafted the plan for far-seeing because they saw that people needed to be prepared in advance in the event of, God forbid, the worst circumstances taking place which did take place. So in my opinion this was a precautionary measure which was both legal and justified and, as such, it could not have caused anything and it could not have caused war either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you look into the Serbian proposal on forming municipalities on the basis of ethnicity wherever there were conditions for that? And were you informed about the proposal that even in the event of conflicts breaking out, whenever Muslims or Croats were able to form their own municipality they should form their municipality and have their own police and administration?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did notice that proposal and it was a very rational one. If you did follow, and you're not a lawyer but a neuropsychologist, but I'm sure you followed the events. In Bosnia and Herzegovina laws on the organisation of municipalities were amended often and municipalities had a tendency to grow larger and larger, so that Serbian municipalities which were mostly rural municipalities would be joined to a town that had a Muslim majority so that you were losing the number of municipalities where Serbs were in a majority. Perhaps the same case applied to Croat municipality. Because for historical reasons, you know you're from Montenegro, I'm from Serbia, Muslims generally lived in towns. Very few of them lived in villages and if they did live in villages they lived along the Drina River. There were practically none along the Sava River. So large swaths of territory were either Serbian and to a degree Croat. So that the organisation of municipalities then was unjust because it joined large Serbian territories with purely Serbian villages and towns to places where the Muslims were in a majority. And so, in my opinion, the separation of Serbian municipalities or the separation of Muslim and Croat municipalities allowed for smaller municipalities but people would be more satisfied and could manage their own affairs more easily. I was born in Banatsko Novo Selo in Banat which had a 7.000 population between the two wars. Two-thirds were Romanians and they had their own municipalities. Now we don't have any municipalities anymore. All of that is counted as Pancevo which has a population of over a hundred thousand. In the same way municipalities were formed in Bosnia so that Serbs, and to a degree Croats, would lose the possibility of living in municipalities where they were in a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you mentioned a decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Now please continue. Please put a pause and speak very slowly, Mr. Cavoski and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, we're rushed for time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a decision by the Constitutional Court which was disputed the Serbian council. How do things stand today in Serbia with the existence of councils for separate ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Serbia is trying to join the European Union, even though I believe that it will never actually join. I -- this is my personal opinion. And the European Union demands the adoption of all -- or recognition of the rights of all ethnic minorities as such, so there we have so-called reverse discrimination. It's called positive action --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not sure this part is relevant. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All I wanted to ask whether this was something that was provided for under the law?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is a council of the Hungarian national minority, the Romanian national minority, a council for the Roma, and they decide on their educational programmes so that they could have their national language and history. They could have a say in that. And through the councils they also run public media which broadcast programmes in the language of that particular ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you talked about a natural state. In Latin that would be "status naturalis"?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us if you had access to the organisation and organised conduct of the Serbian population particularly during the first year of the war? And what can you tell us about that? And could you tell us what the basis for this action was? Did Serbs have any other options and how did this -- how was this conduct presented in these two reports?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I cannot say that the Serbs were a bit naive as opposed to Muslims and Croats who had planned everything well, but it's a fact that the Muslims and the Croats had formed their military units much before the Serbs, and as these military units were not in existence in accordance with the laws and the constitution I would characterise them as paramilitary units. It is a fact that these two authors only qualified the Croatian units as paramilitary, whereas the Muslim units are qualified as the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which I think is not fair but that is the position they have taken. The Serbs relied on the Yugoslav People's Army, and when there were no sufficient recruits due to the war in Croatia -- even though everyone was called up, the Muslims and the Croats and the Serbs, it was mostly the Serbs who responded to the call-ups and joined the ranks of the Yugoslav People's Army. It was only when Milosevic - which in my view was a mistake - accepted the Vance-Owen Plan for the Serbs in Croatia, the then-Serbian Republic of Krajina as it was called, it happened that the Yugoslav People's Army was supposed to pull out of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was only then that the Army of Republika Srpska was set up. As far as I know - and I'm sure you know it better than me - the Serbian side never allowed the activities of any paramilitary units, that is to say highway robbers and others who supposedly waged an ethnic war but plundered private property. So from the very beginning it was well-organised and under strict discipline. So from that point of view the Serbian army met all the criteria set by international law when the civil war is at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us from the point of view of the then-laws, especially the Law on All People's Defence and social self-protection and in view of the nature of the natural state, did the Serbian side have less detrimental resolutions? What options could it choose from and, in your view, did the Serbian side act lawfully or unlawfully when it defended its own survival?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: President Karadzic, you raised a difficult issue and it's the issue of the efficiency of laws and the constitution. The question which arose was: Should one blindly trust the efficiency of the constitution which was then in force and the laws which were then in force or should one be cautious and do something else as well? To digress a little bit, I believe this will be interesting for those who are prisoned. It was a polemics between Sir Edward Coke and Thomas Hobbes. At some point in the 17th century Sir Edward Coke advocated the idea of the rule of law, whereas Thomas Hobbes wondered how the other could say that at all. And he responded in this way: Who has ever heard, he said, that paper and ink can rule without people's swords because the laws are written in ink on paper. So, you see, without adequate force - and that's the military force - even the best constitution is powerless and serious people must know this. So in my view, at least we in Serbia and there were probably also many Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina who reasoned in this way, we have the constitutional order, the constitution mustn't be violated, and so on, whereas the others took measures in a timely fashion to organise themselves. Fortunately the Serbs in the last moment decided to do something and the result were the Crisis Staffs and changing the remains of the former Yugoslav People's Army and these were the soldiers who had been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were now turned into the Army of Republika Srpska so that the soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska were almost exclusively natives of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your opinion did the Serbian side have the right to organise itself and put up resistance to unilateral acts of the Muslim armed forces, or did it have to accept the fait accompli and accept the situation that was imposed on this community?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, the question of legal validity is one thing, and the question whether something made sense or not is different. There are people who are cowards and who would accept everything in order to save their lives which I resolutely reject as a responsible man. In my view, the constitution of some sort of Bosnia-Herzegovina in violation of the constitutional rules of the then-Yugoslavia was an anti-constitutional act. No rights could be drawn from this anti-constitutional act. From the Roman law onwards there is the right -- ex turpi causa non oritur actio, from lack of right, no right can be drawn. So if you have an unlawful establishment of some sort of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you cannot then draw from that a legitimate right to rule over the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other way around. Those who were still acting in observance of the constitution of the former Yugoslavia for the purpose of their own survival, had the moral right, a legitimate right, to organise themselves and to oppose this even if this was not something that was specifically written anywhere in the laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber what you learned during the period in which you chaired the international committee on establishing the truth about Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: At the time when you were already hiding and when it was unknown where you were, to be frank I thought that you were abroad because that would have been the best for you but unfortunately you were not there, there was an idea to constitute a committee on establishing the truth about Dr. Radovan Karadzic, even though there were people who had the greater right than me to do that like the academician Rajko Petrov Nogo or Gojko Djogo who were also your personal friends. People believed that the chairman should be someone who had not really been close with you in his life, and therefore I was appointed. Of course I could not reject this because I didn't want to look as if I were frightened. I would never allow myself to look like that, even though this was a very responsible position. So we constituted this committee on establishing the truth on Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Many well-known people were the members such as the academician Vasilije Krestic, who was one of our best known historians, or Professor Akmadzic, also a member of the academy of arts and sciences, who for a long time used to teach in Sarajevo. There were other renown persons such as Elena Guskova, and so on and so forth. And we then attempted to give lectures, to attend conferences, appear in the media, and explain what we believed to be the truth in your case. We also engaged in publishing business. I was the editor, that is to say at one and the same time the publisher of your works in six volumes in both the Serbian and the English languages so that this is available to everyone. I believe it has to be found in the archives of this Tribunal because this shows what were all the documents that you signed, what were the orders you issued, what were the interviews you gave during this time before you disappeared from the political scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any declarations result in this work which had to do with the indictment against me?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: There were many nice initiatives to do something of the kind. We were joined by several scholarly associates, Vice-President Radulovic, who was an economist, and who drew up two powerful declarations which requested the withdrawing of the indictments that had already been issued against you and which were signed by the most respected people, such as the then-patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church Pavle. This was published in several languages in a beautiful edition and was available to the public at large. I believe that this had a great impact on our public for the simple reason that the signatories guaranteed by their honour that this act had been fully justified. It's a different issue that the indictments were not withdrawn and that we are today sitting at the trial against you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, if we have sufficient time I would call up these two documents in the e-court or would you suggest that we do that after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are starting this session without the witness since there's a matter I would like to deal with in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, while we are waiting for the witness the Chamber ordered on the 5th of 2013 -- 5th of April, 2013, that the report of Kosta Cavoski be redacted in line with its decision. While the Chamber notes the relevant portions of the report have been redacted, the associated footnotes still remain. So therefore, the Chamber instructs the Defence to further redact the associated footnotes in line with the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I advised Dr. Karadzic as a formal matter to show the report to the witness and have him identify it so that it could be admitted, but if that's not necessary we would ask that that report be admitted. It's 1D6911 as redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it's a formality or not, but I'd like Dr. Karadzic to do that. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please show 1D7731 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is 7731 which is one of the declarations the witness had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can show one image because this is bilingual. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Cavoski, could you please tell the Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps page 2 because page 1 is in colour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a declaration which we signed and which requested the withdrawal of indictments against you. And as far as I can see, I have the text in English language here in front of me. A number of reasons are listed there under different items. It was signed by many respectable people and that can be seen in the end, but we cannot see the end here. If we showed the end, we could see the names of at least the first few signatories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just leaf through it.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, here, for example, Professor Smilja Avramov, academician; Ivan Maksimovic; Pavle Ivic; Dejan Medakovic; they're all academicians; Niksa Stipcevic, as well; and in the very end Professor Kosta Cavoski. I was not yet a member of the academy at the time. It seems that we were listed alphabetically but it's not quite right because it's in the Latin alphabet whereas we use the Cyrillic script normally. So about one half of the signatories are members of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just briefly tell us what is the bibliography of these people or their works and careers. Starting with Professor Avramov, what is her position in international law?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I would excuse myself, first of all, because it's not justified for me to speak about myself, but as for the others they are the best and most respected people in Belgrade and in Serbia. Smilja Avramov, for example, is the best-known internationalist, that is to say, an expert in international law; Ivan Maksimovic is a well-known economist; Academician Pavle Ivic used to be our best dialectologist, he was an expert for the Serbian language and its dialects; Dejan Medakovic was the president of the academy of arts and sciences and he's a well-known expert in the history of paintings, primarily frescos, he also wrote about history; Niksa Stipcevic is an expert for romance languages, primarily the Italian language and so on; Academician Vasilije Krestic is our best-known historian; Miodrag Jovicic used to be a friend of mine and he taught constitutional law and political system; then Milorad Ekmecic, an even better known historian who was teaching for a long time in Sarajevo; Mihailo Markovic was our best-known philosopher. Internationally he published dozens of books, most of them in English language, and he was the only philosopher who was more or less known internationally and could teach anywhere. So these are the people who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you assess their position and standing during the one-party system?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As for myself and most of the people listed here, we were very critical of Slobodan Milosevic from the moment when he really came to power in 1987 when he toppled Ivan Stambolic and remained the only one to rule because he did not want to introduce more democracy into the then-system in Serbian. Most of us, not all though, were in opposition. Some of the signatories believed that he could possibly resolve the Serb issue. And so for a while they co-operated with him, as for example Smilja Avramov, but as soon as she saw that he was not pursuing a reasonable policy she left him. Among these people is also Academician Professor Ljubomir Tadic, the father of Boris Tadic, who was our previous president of the republic. He was one of the founders of the democratic party, together with me, the first opposition party in Serbia and Yugoslavia which we founded in November 1989. I was talking about Ljubomir Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And before Slobodan Milosevic in the previous regime, what was the standing and position of these people vis-a-vis the one-party communist regime?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As early as in 1968 and onwards when we had big student demonstrations, opposition was being formed but it was not real opposition because it was not allowed. We were called dissidents. That was typical of eastern Europe in that era. So most of these people were from the ranks of the dissidents, as for example Mihailo Markovic. He was a well-known member of the Praxis club. There were eight of them who were thrown out of the faculty of philosophy and then employed in some sort of institute and so on. They were in disgrace during the then-regime but they were prominent experts and they were well-known abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this declaration please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3378, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D7732 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have 24 signatories here; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: June 1996. Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: This is the second declaration requesting the abolishment of proceedings before ICTY against Dr. Radovan Karadzic, once again published in four languages. It is similar to the previous one in terms of contents. There are some changes, of course. I just wonder whether the signatories are different, but we can see at the very end if we show the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please leaf through it in one language until we reach the last page.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, we can do it in English, no problem at all. Now we only have it in Serbian but the Chamber cannot ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we leaf through it until we can see the signatures?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, until we see the signatures but the English version would be better because then the honourable Chamber could also follow. Yes. Here there are 60 signatures, so the number is significantly bigger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just leave the English version on the screen, please, and collapse the Serbian and then zoom into the version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in addition to those who had signed the previous declaration we can see here many more new people who are well-known and well respected or were at the time. Unfortunately many of them are among the dead now. For example, Enriko Josif, a well-known composer and a member of the Serbian academy of arts and science. He is Jewish. Enriko Josif, I knew him personally. He was a great man, and so on. Or, for example, Slavko Gavrilovic, he's also new here, a member of the academy. Dragoslav Mihailovic, also a member of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences, a well-known writer, a novelist who devoted a great part of his life to Goli Otok because he had been a detainee at Goli Otok. He was jailed there for a number of years. So these are the signatories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And at the top?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: At the very top is the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church Pavle. You see, he always signed his name with a cross which is typical of high-ranking church dignatory. Serbian patriarch Pavle, that was his title. He is the first and then other 60 signatures follow. Sixty-one in total. This is the proof of what I said earlier that the Serbian patriarch Pavle signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this declaration also be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3379, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 1D06911.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now please tell us what this document is that we see.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: This is the report I wrote for your trial: "A critical analysis of the works of Robert J. Donia and Patrick J. Treanor and secession within the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina." It's a report prepared for your trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us how these two experts understood and presented the legitimate rights of the Serbian people or the Serbian authorities; in other words, how they treated the Muslim and Croatian sides and how they treated the Serbian side from the point of view of legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I will try to be brief because we should leave some time to the Prosecutor for the cross-examination. Speaking about the Serbian leaders, including you as president, both use the phrase "nationalists" or "nationalist delegates" or "nationalist positions." In the English language that is derogatory. Speaking about the Muslims, they never used this word. Instead, they say activists, Muslim activists. And speaking about the Croats, the words "nationalist" and "nationalistic" are used only when Croats negotiate with Serbs about the alleged division of Bosnia. Here I refer first and foremost to the talks that you as president of the RS had with Mate Boban in Grac, the latter was president of Herceg-Bosna. This was the third separate unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Mate Boban when he negotiates with the Serbs without the Muslims is called a nationalist. However, when Croats negotiate with the Muslims without the Serbs, that's considered fully legitimate and no such derogatory term is used. And at the very end of the war under the influence of the USA, Alija Izetbegovic, Franjo Tudjman, and a representative of the Bosnian Croats met to craft the so-called Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, an entity without Serbs in the framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and decided that this Federation would be part of a confederation with Croatia. So this was a project going beyond the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was not a problem to these two, but rather something normal. I believe that this can be seen as a belittling attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us how under the conditions of the breakup of the single sovereignty to -- into three ethnic sovereignties where the application of force, was it all right to call them the government and call -- whereas us we were called the Bosnian Serbs. Did they have the right to do that or did we have the right to sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I had been promised to be brief in order to leave some time for the Prosecution. When the Presidency of Yugoslavia shrunk from eight members to four, all international factors refused to co-operate with it. However, when it comes to the Bosnian Presidency which had seven members, the Serbs were the first to leave it, followed by the Croats which makes for a total of four members, and finally Abdic in the Cazin Krajina refused to attend, and as a consequence was evicted from the Presidency by an illegitimate decision. However, Robert Donia and Patrick Treanor qualified this remaining body the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although their term in office of one year had already elapsed so that under the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina somebody else should have succeeded the president of the Presidency. However, the president remained the same until the Dayton Accord and Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I stand accused, that is, the Serbian side, and I in particular, for ethnic cleansing and the permanent removal of Muslims and Croats from the territories we consider aren't fully ours. Did you see any evidence or any indication that the Serbian side refused refugees to return once peace had set in?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I haven't seen anything like that in -- when I studied the documents. I saw no written declaration or oral statement to the effect that anybody from the leading circles of the RS stated anything of the kind. On the contrary, it was always understood that refugees would return and finally that became part of the Dayton Accord, too. After the war I lectured at the faculty of law in eastern Sarajevo. I was personally in the position to see that people were, indeed, returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were aware that we were giving in, making concessions, accepting various plans, did you see any evidence that the Serbian side had plans that could not be implemented otherwise than by using force and committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I have never seen such evidence. I personally think that a large part of the combat activities were carried out for self-defence and for the preservation of your own identity. When war is waged, that is done with a goal in mind and that goal was the preservation of the Serbian ethnicity and the preservation of life and property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this neutrally and in a unbiased manner presented in these two reports?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Certainly not. Let's take the example of Sarajevo. Speaking about Muslim victims, their numbers are always stated. However, when the Serbian victims in Sarajevo itself are mentioned then no numbers are mentioned. They -- it is said that they -- there were about 150, although there were maybe as many as 3.000. The perpetrators were never mentioned. Before the courts in the Federation of BiH or here before this Tribunal, the responsible persons are not mentioned but however when it comes to the Serbs then names are always given. This applies also to exchange of artillery fire, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this expert report. We will revise the footnotes in connection with the paragraphs that were deleted and the remainder is hereby tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with the proper redactions, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3380, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I have no further questions for Professor Cavoski. I'll wait for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a quick question for clarification. This report itself includes Dr. Cavoski's CV, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the last page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Before I get into some of the details of your report, I'll just follow-up on a few of the questions that Mr. Karadzic asked you during the examination-in-chief. First of all, with respect to the issue he raised during the very last part of the examination about the implementation of plans that required force, let me ask you this: Did you ever see any evidence, Professor, that the Bosnian Serb leadership or Bosnian Serb forces sought territory, for example, for strategic reasons on which Muslims were a majority?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I personally saw no such evidence, although I travelled around Bosnia-Herzegovina even during the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
