utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I'm not talking about your -- I see you're answering in terms of your personal observations only. I'm -- and I'll let you finish that, but I had in mind also documents you reviewed for purposes of your report or any other reason.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I can start answering to your second question. I mostly focused on the analysis of these two reports and I did not analyse many other documents which I did in my earlier works. I set myself the task here to criticise these two reports item by item with special consideration of the constitutionality aspect. I didn't deal with other matters because that was not my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. That may give me an indication of what answer I can expect to my next questions. But let me follow-up on something else that Mr. Karadzic asked you and that is about attitudes toward population transfers. Do you know with whom Professor Koljevic met on or about January 8th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was able to infer from this report, he met Tudjman or his men in Zagreb. Either Donia or Patrick Treanor cites some documents from that meeting. Nikola Koljevic as the vice-president of the RS was there in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Among other things, territorial issues were discussed such as the Croats in the Posavina and elsewhere and the attitude toward the Muslims. That's what the reports of these two gentlemen say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it you know it from those reports, and do I take it that you don't recall from your own review of the transcript of that meeting discussion about population transfers and the aim of national homogeneity?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That certainly was one of the issues raised, but it had to do with Serbo-Croatian relations. I must say - but you probably know it just as I do - when borders are drawn then the so-called process of opting is applied -- is implemented. I was born in Banat and when the border between the then-Yugoslavia and Romania was drawn, the Serbs who left on the Romanian side could opt to be transferred to the Serbian side and vice versa. But something like that was understood here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me indicate some basic ground rules to you. We'll both try to abide by those. I don't want to interrupt you when you're in the course of answering a question I've asked. At the same time, I have to be mindful of the time I've been allotted and the efficient running of the courtroom. So if I consider that you've strayed outside the boundaries of the question, I will interrupt and mention that. Okay? Do you know what was discussed at a meeting in Doboj on or about February 13th, 1992, attended by members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. That's reflected in evidence we've received in court, but if you don't, and that's P3474, but if you don't know that I won't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Tieger add that the Defence considers the Brdjanin reports about what was allegedly said fake. It would be fair to put that to both the Chamber and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's an absurd, with all respect in the context of the courtroom, intervention. I didn't inquire about that because the witness didn't indicate any knowledge of it. We could have discussed that if we had entered into any discussion of the area, but now this is a -- simply commentary by the accused that is quite unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was not following either, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was considerable discussion during the course of your examination-in-chief, Witness, about the Cutileiro Plan. And I noted that at page 29 of your report you mention the Cutileiro Plan and - as you do in many parts of your report - criticise Professor Donia for allegedly failing to give all the facts about the Cutileiro Plan that you consider should be made. And in particular, he notes that, at page 95 through 96 of his report, "Bosnian Serb Leadership and the Siege of Sarajevo," that the three parties agreed to keep principles of the Cutileiro Plan as it became known as a basis for further negotiations, but they did not sign the agreement. And among the things you criticise him for is the fact that the Cutileiro Plan was not signed but it was initialled. And you -- that's the first sentence in the initiation of your criticism of Professor Donia for that excerpt of his report. Now, you also testified in the Galic case about the Cutileiro Plan and that was back in 2003, and at that time you actually made the assertion that the Cutileiro Plan was signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That it was initialled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well -- and I'll read you what you said in Galic, and that's at page 19133 of 65 ter 24943. And you start discussing the various plans, but when the European Union engaged the Portuguese diplomat Jose Cutileiro to negotiate with all three sides, Alija Izetbegovic participated in this himself and he signed that plan too. And then the question was asked: "I'd be very grateful if you could tell us very briefly what happened after the signing of this agreement." And your answer began: "When this plan was signed ..." So at that time, sir, you were making the assertion that, in fact, the plan had been signed and that was your position as an expert witness based on your careful review of all the documents; right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I must first say that I'm a bit surprised by the fact that you are now referring to my report in the Galic case while at the same time disputing my right to analyse Robert Donia's report in other cases. Unfortunately I don't have that report before me, but I trust that what you read is correct. Talking about the signing, the declaration on constitutional principles was signed, it really was, but the plan couldn't be signed because it wasn't completed. A comprehensive plan is signed which apart from the constitutional principles includes also the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian municipalities, and it explicitly states that the remaining contested issues -- and even the Prosecutor criticised me for saying that some municipalities had a Serbian majority, confronting me with a census from 1993 or 1994, as a result of which those municipalities did not have a Serbian majority. As a lawyer I know perfectly well that such a document can only be signed once this division is signed, but the constitutional principles really were signed and it contains the way of the constitution of the three entities within Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the difference between initialling and signing, I would like to remind you that the Dayton Accord was initialled at Dayton and signed in Paris, although it was the very same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what Dr. Karadzic said about the March 18th agreement in principles at the time? Did you look at what he said, for example, to the Bosnian Serb Assembly about that document?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I even published it but I certainly cannot remember each and every detail. I think that the agreement, although the Serbs reluctantly accepted it eventually did accept it after all because they wanted to preserve the peace. But I don't remember his exact words. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me quote his exact words, and this is at D90 at about page 5: "The document has been accepted as a basis as a foundation for further negotiations. The document has not been signed. We would never sign anything that we did not agree upon." And then further, at page 43 in English and page 62 in Serbian: "What we have here is a process ..." And then Dr. Karadzic continues: "We have entered into this process with our strategic goals and we are accomplishing them stage by stage. We would never have signed this paper as a document, never, never, never, but at this stage it would be crazy not to accept it." And then at page 46 in the English and page 66 through 67 in the Serbian: "Rest assured," quoting again, "there will be no signing before we have achieved what we want and you all know our strategic plans ..." And then I'll continue with that in a moment. So those are the words of Dr. Karadzic contemporaneously. Your criticism of Dr. Donia for asserting that there was an agreement on March 18th but that the document was not signed is, in fact, completely consistent with what Dr. Karadzic was reassuring the Bosnian Serb Assembly at the time it was taking place; correct? And that's simply something that you overlooked?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No, I didn't overlook it at all. In the media at the time, at least in Belgrade, it was presented as agreed that the constitutional principles had been agreed upon and that the only thing remaining was the division of municipalities between these through [as interpreted] entities. That was what I knew at the time. I never had any document in my hands that bears signatures, unlike you. I only relied upon what was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- thank you for that, but you criticised Dr. Donia. In the spirit of his standard practice, you say, he failed to give all the facts, the Cutileiro Plan was not signed but it was initialled. Dr. Donia said it wasn't signed. Dr. Karadzic at the time emphasised that it wasn't signed, and yet you're acting as if Dr. Donia is somehow withholding a critical factor.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: What I criticised Donia for is something much more far-reaching. He didn't want to present the importance of these talks and the possible outcome of peace in Bosnia at the price of serious concessions by the Serbs. This is my crucial criticism of Donia, and I believe I'm right in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right, because Dr. Karadzic had from very early stages of his political career said that if the Bosnia -- if Bosnia moved towards sovereignty and independence, that was something that the SDS and the Bosnian Serb leadership would not accept and war would result, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. I said that there were three levels of concessions from the Serbian side. The first request by the Serbian side was the survival of Yugoslavia, and as a lawyer you know very well that this demand is a legitimate one, to preserve the already-existing state which is now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor, I will interrupt you because I'm -- sorry, let's try to keep it focused.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've already talked about what you understand the gradations of concession to be and what they may have -- what the Cutileiro Plan may have represented. What I was asking you, and let me put it a slightly different way, are you aware of any expressions by the accused, by Dr. Karadzic, well before the -- either the recognition of sovereignty and independence by the international community or the Cutileiro Plan to the effect that he and the Bosnian Serb leadership would not accept any move toward sovereignty and independence of Bosnia, any move that would separate Serbs in Bosnia from Serbs outside Bosnia by a border and that the Serbs were strong and would prevent that from happening, that war would result? Are you aware of any expressions like that, for example, in 1990?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, I was also saying that in 1990. But you know it's one set of circumstances in 1990 and then another one in 1991, but did anyone expect in 1990 that powerful international factors, the United States and the then-European Community, would recognise any type of secession? All of them were in favour of preserving the integrity of Yugoslavia, and so in such circumstances it's normal, not just for Karadzic but for myself as well, to assert that Yugoslavia must not be broken up and that this must be opposed by force in a manner that is legitimate and that is by using the Yugoslav armed forces, the Yugoslav People's Army. So at that point in time in 1990 that was quite a normal thing. In 1990 we still didn't know what would happen. There were these meetings of the presidents of the republics and the provinces who travelled for meetings to different provinces, and you know that very well. This was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It -- thank you, Professor. It would have sufficed if you had said, yes, you were familiar with such pronouncements. But you've now expressed your point. With respect to the Cutileiro Plan, both today and in your report, you also suggest that there was very little left to do after the agreement on principle because there was -- all that remained was the -- were negotiations over the delineation of territory. And you said both, if I recall your report correctly, that you considered that there was no interest in contiguous territories by the Bosnian Serbs and that the resolution of the borders of the Bosnian Serb entity would be based on negotiations involving a majority presence in various places. Now, with that in mind, let me ask you if you were familiar with any expressions -- if you are familiar with any expressions by the accused at that time to the effect that the Bosnian Serbs had certain strategic objectives that involved linkage to Serbia, that Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leaders wanted to make the Bosnian Serb entity as large as it could be, and that the determination of how large the Bosnian Serb entity would eventually be would depend on conditions that were established by the Bosnian Serb officials on the ground. Are you familiar with expressions like that, that the delineation of territory was going to involve, among other things, the actual conditions which the officials on the ground would create?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell the witness exactly which point of time you're talking about. Is it war, before the war? Is it something that was stated at the Assembly? Could you please give the context to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tieger said "at that time."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right, and if there's any doubt about it I'm talking about the time of the Cutileiro Plan negotiations, February/March 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As for the strategic goals and linkage, it's a fact that all three sides had that intention, not just the Serbs but the Croats that were thinking of linking up with Croatia, which is logical; and of course Muslims who wanted to be as compact as possible, so their problem was that Cazin Krajina which is separated and cut off by municipalities populated by either Croat or Serb majorities. Thus, all three sides were taking that into account and I have to tell you I'm seriously studying politics, I've been observing people for a long number of years, you must make a fine difference between a man who is sitting down and negotiating with Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban about this division. And another thing is when each of them is addressing their own National Assembly. I remember very well that Dr. Radovan Karadzic, the president of Republika Srpska, held a speech before the Assembly of Republika Srpska seeking the support for the Vance-Owen Plan and the Assembly rejected that. And I know why he did that because he was forced to sign conditionally that agreement in Greece because of pressure by strong international factors, primarily Slobodan Milosevic. So what a politician does is important not so much what he says. There's a famous novel by Mesa Selimovic where the main character says that a man is what he does and what he speaks. So always an action must follow words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you do not consider when a political leader turns to his followers and says: The only remaining question is one of quantity and it will happen according to our political will, our right to self-determination and organisation. It will happen according to the actual conditions which are up to you to create, that that's not an act. That's only words that can be ignored. As an expert, you wouldn't even pay attention to that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. When we're talking about politics, the force of will and resolve is very important and it has to be awakened and this is the purpose of speeches and you will notice that always there is a minor difference between what is said and what is eventually done. I said in relation to the Vance-Owen Plan where Dr. Karadzic advocated conditionally its acceptance, but the People's Assembly rejected that by a majority. And as you can see there's always the discrepancy between what he was saying and what he actually did. I also think that if you were carefully observing or monitoring the speeches of Slobodan Milosevic, he promised a lot that he did not actually manage to achieve. As for Karadzic, in my opinion, he was much more consistent in that regard. But for sure when he's addressing his own people and the National Assembly, he tried to encourage them, to give some impetus and this is the objective of political speeches. But as for what was going on at negotiations, the municipalities that were planned, and sometimes if you cannot find a solution for certain municipalities that are disputed, then you would tend to accept the arbitrage of the European Community and I think that was an honourable and honest way to resolve things at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So do I take it that you were familiar or you were not familiar with Dr. Karadzic telling the members of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, telling the municipality presidents, telling delegates who were from various municipalities that the quantity of the entity would depend upon the actual conditions which were up to them to create? Yes or no, did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. As far as that goes, I knew that for sure because I was drafting, I was editing, all of his speeches for publication. And as I was editing the speeches both in Serbian and in English, I read this several times but I did not expect you to discuss these things. So I'm not prepared. I would have brought with me the report that I had prepared for the trial of General Galic. You asked as the Prosecutor for those parts to be cut out of my report that relate to other court proceedings --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to stop you. I'll ask you a few questions right now about material in your report. Let's turn to page 41 of your report.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, here at page 41 you focus on what you assert was the malevolent insertion of the word "commander" in a discussion about the -- and here: "Robert Donia malevolently inserted the word 'commander' in the sentence." That is -- and the sentence is: "Local SDS leaders were instructed to form an Assembly of the Serb people and a Crisis Staff of the Serb people" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, let's identify the page number first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's 41 still on the same page, Mr. President, 41 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, let's -- sorry, let's allow the Chamber to catch up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the B/C/S and the English are matching.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right, Professor, it is the part of your report that discusses page 20 of Dr. Donia's "Bosnian Serb Leadership and the Siege of Sarajevo" report and it's about -- okay.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: [In English] 42, yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, thanks. And it's 41 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the impugned sentence is: "Local SDS leaders were instructed to form an 'assembly of the Serb people' and a 'Crisis Staff of the Serb people,' which was to be headed by a 'commander.'" And you assert there, as you do in various parts of your report, that this was a malevolent act by Dr. Donia, inserting the word "commander" in that sentence. Now, can we agree, Professor, that the context of this sentence in Dr. Donia's report is a discussion of the Variant A and B document, the 19 December 1991 instructions?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: First of all, you did not say here what was important and that is that the word "komandant," commander does not exist in Serbian. In footnote J on page 106 it only says Crisis Staff of the Serbian people call and convene an Assembly of the Serbian people. He inserted the word "komandant" there even though that word is not in the Serbian text that he quotes in his footnote J. I know Serbian and Robert Donia knows Serbian quite well. So he could not have made an error unless he meant to do so. So he inserted a word that does not exist in the Serbian version. This is my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you see this, Professor? This is the instruction of the organisations and activities of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in emergency conditions dated 19 December 1991, otherwise known as Variant A and B document, that you testified in the last session you read very carefully. That's P03470.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what it states at page 3 of the English, that's in option A, first stage, is the following: "The president of the Municipal Assembly or the president of the Municipal Executive Board shall be the commander of the Crisis Staff. The commander shall" --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload it so the witness can follow. Page number, Mr. Tieger? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That should be page 3 of both, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's toward the top of the page, Professor, and as I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay: "The president of the Municipal Assembly or the president of the Municipal Executive Board shall be the commander of the Crisis Staff. "The commander shall appoint a member of the Crisis Staff as co-ordinator for relations with the municipal leaderships of the SDA ..." And it goes on to describe the other aspects of preparation. Similarly, for the -- for option B municipalities it states at page 5 of both again, I believe: "The president of the Municipal Assembly of the SDS" -- sorry, for you, Professor, it will be 6 through 7. So if we can turn to page 6 and it will continue on to the next page as well. "The president of the Municipal Assembly of the SDS shall be the commander of the Crisis Staff. "The commander shall appoint a member of the Crisis Staff as co-ordinator for relations with the municipal leaderships of the SDA and HDZ ..." And it goes on to discuss the convening and proclamation of the Assembly of the Serbian people, preparations for the take-over of staff, et cetera, et cetera. So, in fact, the document that you claimed about an hour ago that you read very carefully contains multiple references to commander, and Dr. Donia's reference to the commander is hardly a malevolent introduction of that phrase. It's an accurate reflection of what the document states; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I'm afraid that you are misinterpreting this place. When I said that he malevolently inserted it, it's because in the footnote on page 106 that term is not mentioned. So he refers to the footnote as a source, what it says in English, and then he adds that it will be headed by a commander. So that footnote does not contain that term and that is why I said that inserting it into the English text was malicious. I don't dispute that the word appears in the original document. Donia could have referred to the original document and could have cited that instead of saying in footnote J that the Crisis Staff of the Serbian people convened an Assembly of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's the kind of evidence you're bringing before this Court, Professor? Even though local SDS leaders were instructed by this document to both form an Assembly of the Serbian people and a Crisis Staff of the Serb people, which in fact it said would be headed by a commander, you now tried to suggest in the report that that assertion in his report is malevolent because that word doesn't appear in the particular footnote, although it is replete in the document itself? That's the nature of your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. I was very analytical and I tried to show that he did not actually follow the Serbian text and that he was inserting words in the English text that were not there in the Serbian text. This is not permissible to anyone, particularly to a historian. A person has to be very careful. When he translates into English he has to translate precisely what is there in the Serbian original. So he did not do that and this is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're talking about significant matters here. You're talking about a significant document. Did you say anywhere in your report to the Bench, to whom you were submitting your report, that, in fact, there is an omission of that word in the footnote but that, in fact, the assertion is correct, that the document itself provides exactly what he says it provides, and that it would -- therefore, if in your view the word "commander" or "komandant" was added to that sentence to represent the Crisis Staff as a military staff, then in fact it was a military staff because the document itself says that? Did you bother to tell the Bench that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: When we're talking about a military staff, we know what a military staff is, it exclusively commands military units. But if we're talking about a staff that manages civilian affairs, such as protection of the population, preparation of food reserves, equipment reserves, health care, and other issues, then this is not a purely military staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, Professor. I'm using your words. You said that that word was entered into the document because Dr. Donia malevolently wanted the Trial Chamber, to whom it was submitted, to consider it as a military staff, which as you say always has a commander. Now we see that in fact the document itself uses the word "commander" repeatedly. So I was just using your words, that therefore we can see that the Crisis Staff is a military staff or at least has a military staff aspect; right? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: It just had the character of a military staff to a certain degree. Hostilities had still not broken out so they were not traditionally in that sense of the word military staffs. Let me repeat this once again, I study history and I know very well how one must formulate citations. It must be absolutely reliable. If somebody cites a source and it's different in a footnote, and so on, if it's done improperly then it throws doubt on his credibility. And since this is something that you are mentioning, for example, in the remainder of the text what was omitted was "Sarajevo, the Biography of a City." But here it was not omitted and then you can see that some parties, some other national parties also formed Crisis Staffs. It's on that same page where -- discussing page 20 is that the most frequent form of such an organ is a Crisis Staff. This is what Donia says in the book "Sarajevo, the Biography of a City," which you requested be edited out of my report but here it remains. Other parties formed Crisis Staffs, but when they're being discussed he does not refer to commanders in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- okay. Let me suggest a couple things to you: Number one, that the -- that exploiting what is, at worst, a typo but which in fact appears to be simply two incorporated references to suggest malevolence itself reflects the bias of the person doing that exploiting. And number two, the discussion here is about the Variant A and B documents, sir, and what you're communicating to the Court about that document and what you're not communicating to the Court about that document. But let's turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I will come to the issue of the reference, Dr. Cavoski, but do you now agree that the Crisis Staff was to be headed or the Crisis Staff was to have a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was provided for in the rules, but that was supposed to be the president of the municipality. The president of the municipality is not military officer. He's not even somebody who went through military training. That is the word that is used, the term, but that does not correspond to the military protocol. As for these remarks of yours in the sense that I also maliciously stated that, I just wanted to say something that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- something at the beginning of my report that has to do with Patrick Treanor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, no we are referring to this part. And can you upload the relevant part of Donia's report. I think it's Exhibit P973. I take it it is e-court page 23 in the middle of paragraph: "Local SDS leaders were instructed to form an 'assembly of the Serb people' and a 'Crisis Staff of the Serb people,' which was to be headed by a 'commander.'" And there's footnote 49 and looking at the footnote itself, I can't follow what you're saying in your report. Could you explain to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I can see after the footnote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We need to see footnote 49 below 48.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please pay attention. After number 49 there is a letter J at the very end. So these are two footnotes. One is footnote 49 and the other one is footnote J which you seem to have missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 49 J, then shall we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not on the next page. It is on page 106 in the text which was available to me, page 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court page 109.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under J. I would ask you to look at J, you will see what is written there in Serbian. There is no "commander." Let me please read it out, under J: "'Crisis Staff of the Serbian people;'" again open quotes, "'convene and pronounce the assembly of the Serbian people.'" So that is the original text, there is no word "commander." That word is not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I followed in full. I'll leave it to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to assist the Court slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Although the specific references to the locations in the report where those aspects are mentioned, including the commander, are reflected in footnote 49 and readily available to you in addition to the entirety of the document itself; right? Or do you not know what [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I focused on the actual footnote which is referred to here, and that is the footnote under J. I do not dispute what the other document says, but this as the footnote provided no basis for using the word "commander." It's simply not allowed. You said that it could have been a typo and I wanted to say something, but the Presiding Judge stopped me. When I mentioned Patrick Treanor's report, I said that these errors, the three errors, were insignificant. He has but few such errors. Unfortunately, Robert Donia has many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to something I think similar, another accusation of malevolence against Dr. Donia. That appears at page 16. And that is the alleged omission or deletion of the negation "not" in the context of something Mr. Krajisnik said in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean page 16 in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, Mr. President, it's page 16 in hard copy and it will be -- it's that part of the report referring to -- well, in any event page 16 in hard copy is the easiest way to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor, it's that part of your report -- okay.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, right. It's page 15. It says here page 7 and it begins under 5: "The second session on the 21st of November, 1991, Krajisnik," and then a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that appears in the report on the thematic excerpts from the Assembly of Republika Srpska; correct? Professor, you were aware, I'm sure, that this report was to be submitted to this Trial Chamber for its review and that the Trial Chamber would be reviewing the document in English; correct? I mean, you're aware of that practice at the institution?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So I presume you went to what was the original of the submission to see whether there was any malevolent effort to fool the Trial Chamber into misunderstanding what Mr. Krajisnik had said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I received a text which included quotations in the Serbian language, and as Donia is quite well-versed in the Serbian I suppose that he had appropriately read it, selected excerpts, and included them in his report. And then I noticed that he omitted the negation which is very significant here because it turns out Krajisnik advocated resolutions that would be to the detriment of other peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that was precisely where the negation should have been included, so I believe that something like that is -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before you accused Professor Donia of malevolence, and I presume malevolence for in your view for trying to mislead the Chamber into thinking that something was the case when it was not, did you bother to check what the submission in English that would actually reach the Court and would read said? Did you bother to do that before making this allegation of malevolence?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I only had the report in Serbian. I believed it to be more truthful because that's the source language. It's a different issue how it was translated into English, especially as errors may happen when something is translated into English. I therefore treated the Serbian text as the source and I only looked at it, and I believe that I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The English text says, Professor, exactly what you -- it has the language that you complain is not there, that is, all the proposed solutions must be based on the constitution and the laws, et cetera, but not at the expense of other peoples. That's what the submission to the Chamber said. Will you admit now there's clearly no malevolence in this, or are you still going to stick by your accusations regarding this passage?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I can only say that if Donia himself translated that into English and I don't think that he did. But it cannot be excluded that the translator concluded that this makes no sense and that Krajisnik said something like that and that he then introduced the negation, no. If Donia had wanted this, he wouldn't have made an error when quoting a Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So what you're trying to tell this Court is -- and you've looked at the rest of the passage; right? Look at the rest of the passage. Because the rest of the passage, I submit to you, makes crystal clear that there -- what Krajisnik is saying, and it says further on: "The basic principle is not to impose the will ..." et cetera, et cetera. "We should respect the legitimate will ...," on and on. So were you trying to suggest that Dr. Donia malevolently omitted the word "not" in the first part of that excerpt but stupidly left in the rest of those negations and the rest of the passage that would make it obvious what Krajisnik was saying? Is that your interpretation of what happened?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: If Professor Donia had made only three errors, which is the number that Patrick Treanor made, then I wouldn't have taken that into account at all. As I said that the insignificant errors made by Patrick Treanor are not important. However, it is quite frequent in his report. I do this in a systematic manner. Unfortunately, great part of my report has been redacted because it mentions the book "Sarajevo, biography," which is not admitted among the documents of this Tribunal, and so forth, as well as other documents. It is quite frequent and I tried whenever I could to see how he came to do that, and whenever I found errors which are frequent then I concluded that he was doing that malevolently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you also accused Mr. Treanor of purposely keeping silent about essential facts, don't you. Let's turn to page 78 of your report. Now, this is the section -- it's the third page of the section that begins: "Avoidance of relevant facts ..." And it's where you're talking about a constituent people and state-building nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify the page number in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That actually makes it slightly difficult, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor, can we [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can compare the footnote numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very good. Footnotes 42, 43, and 44 appear on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to be the next page -- I'm not sure. Yes, please go on. Continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your criticism there, Professor, focuses on the following passage of Dr. Treanor's report: "The constitution dropped the reference in Croatia's constitution to the Serbs as one of the constituent peoples of the republic, although it did not guarantee national equality in Article 3 ..." And that's an example of what you allege is keeping silent about essential facts because, as you explain, he should have used the expression "state-building nation." Now, in that connection, that is, the allegations you raise about the matters I've just described, tell me if this sounds familiar, Professor: "Q. Were parts of the constitution changed? "A. Well, first of all, there was the amendment number 60 which was introduced. It didn't change anything as far as the constitutionality, the constituent nature of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina was concerned, and this concerned the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims. First of all, the constitution was respected and then later it was respected less and less. So the Muslim side within the common authorities tried to obtain independence, and one of the constituent peoples opposed such independence and that constituent people, they were the Serbs." Lots of references to constituent peoples there, Professor. Is that also -- does that also represent the practice of omitting -- staying silent about essential facts?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, now we are discussing an issue that I'm well-versed with because I'm an expert for constitutional law. Some words, even when they are of foreign origin --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor, unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: -- when they're adopted in a language --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have to answer my question, sir. Before -- I'll -- I'll give you a chance to explain nuances if it's necessary, but I want an answer to my question. Is the passage I read to you another example of keeping silent about essential facts because it uses repeatedly the expression "constituent peoples" rather than "state-building nation"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we know where this comes from. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is it in the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- kindly stop his helpful intrusions. It's very obvious by now what he's trying to do repeatedly, and he needs to be admonished about that strongly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's unnecessary, it's unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could give the reference --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary at all. It's not necessary for anyone to assist me. I'm telling you that the word "constituent" has a quite specific meaning in the Serbo-Croatian language. It means basically state building. And when you say in the English language "constituent," it just means integral, an integral part of something else and nothing more than that. Therefore, as Patrick Treanor very well knows, as he knows the Serbian language very well, he knows what the constituent knows in our constitutional legal terminology, he had to make sure to formulate it well in the English language. Because when you say it like this, that the Serbs are one of the constituent peoples, then it turns out in the Serbian language that they are one of the peoples that make part of this. And it's quite a different sense when you say that Serbs in addition to the Croatian people are a state-building nation, and this is why I chose this particular formulation, "state-building."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So is it correct then that the passage I just read out to you is another example of keeping silent about essential facts because it uses the term "constituent peoples" repeatedly rather than "state-building nation"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for the reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Croatia, this was of major significance because the Croats denied this to the Serbs, and as --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, no, if you can't answer the question just tell me, but I don't want another dissertation on [overlapping speakers]... between the two terms.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You can answer. That's what I'm asking you to do [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. President, excuse me, Mr. Tieger can't shut down the witness like that. That is -- not only is it impolite but it's unfair. So I would ask that maybe we could take a lunch break so Mr. Tieger can take a breath and calm down, but we have to treat the witnesses here like professionals and that is not occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before taking the lunch break let's hear the witness, but it's fair to give the reference what you recited, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President, but then it will be clear why I was asking for an answer before I did so and what I believe Dr. Karadzic is doing. And, if I may say, I believe it is impolite for a witness to avoid questions. I believe it's perfectly appropriate to urge a witness to focus on a question, and I believe it's also an obligation on the part of an examiner to bring that to the witness's attention. So I reject Mr. Robinson's efforts to stop me from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So this reference that I made --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second, I think it's perfectly good timing to take a lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may -- all right. I'd like to continue with the -- follow-up on the Court's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue after the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 17 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor, just before the break we were quietly discussing page 78 of your report, and I had asked you about a particular quote involving the repeated references to constituent peoples. I don't know if you've thought it over in the break and can answer me, but my question was whether or not those repeated references to constituent peoples without using the expression "state-building nation" represented another example of keeping silent about essential facts?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I will very gladly answer this question of yours. You see, the question is what is the context in which this is mentioned? He's dealing with Croatia and the Croats actually adopted a new constitution from which they deleted the provision that the Serbs were a state-building nation because they deleted a provision from earlier constitutions which said that Croatia was a state of the Croatian and the Serbian peoples. More or less that was the provision. That was quite important. And in that context, it was very important because Serbs made up 12.5 per cent of the population in Croatia before the breakout of the war and it was very important for them to keep the status of state-building nation. When you let someone know that it's not so important, then it would be sufficient to guarantee equality of nations. Under item 3, I can tell you that this is not sufficient because equality of nations only means the equality of citizens as such as compared to other nations. And when you talk about the state building, then what one has in mind is the equality of the collective as such with relation to the other collective which makes up this state. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can see I'm not going to get a yes or no answer to my question and I will leave it at that, except to note in response to, as I would have noted in any event and also in response to the accused's question, that the passage I quoted, and I will submit it to the Court, appears at page 19110 through 19111 of your testimony in the Galic case and that is your response to a question posed to you during that case during which you repeatedly used the expression "constituent peoples" and not the expression "state-building nation." If you -- I take it you don't remember your testimony, but perhaps you can confirm that you said that.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, let me explain what the major difference is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, sir -- I have -- if it's your position that there's a difference between the two and the accused wants to get into the nature of that difference, that's fine. So you've indicated you consider there is a difference between your use of the words constituent peoples and Mr. Treanor's use of the words constituent peoples. I will leave it at that and move on in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think the witness has a right to explain it this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have spent ten minutes with this witness explaining the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] We can ask the witness to confirm whether he said so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina where it was not denied to a single people whether it was a constituent people or not, it was fully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Dr. Cavoski, do you remember the question? Whether you testified as cited by Mr. Tieger in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian language I used the formulation "konstitutivni narod," constituent people. We used this expression in Serbian and we know what it means. How that was interpreted into English that was not up to me because I am not an interpreter or translator, or nor did I translate my own text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understand the answer. Let's proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor, at page 13 of your report and for your ease of reference --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: [In English] Just a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I have a question for the interpreters or can we upload the B/C/S version. If we translate English word "constituent people" or "constituent nation," is it translated into other words or the same words?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It depends on the nuances but there is an expression in the Serbian language which is "konstitutivni narod" and that is the closest interpretation of "constituent people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave it at that and I will leave it for the parties to take up the issue further if necessary -- no, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may suggest, you might request from the interpreters to interpret for you the Serbian word "drzavotvorni." What are the ways it can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can take that issue in your re-examination. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor this is a reference to the following excerpt from Dr. Donia's report. On 28 March, the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia voted to enact constitutional amendments that eliminated most of Kosovo's autonomy within the republic. That's shortly after your first reference to the origins of Republika Srpska background report, page 5 of that report. Do you find that? Okay. I see you have that. There you state -- you criticise Dr. Donia for invoking an unreliable source and then at the end of that critique of what Dr. Donia did assert that he believed as true the quote of a publicist who probably heard or read somewhere what he wrote. Now, the person you refer to as a publicist is cited at the beginning of that passage by Dr. Donia and that's of Cohen who wrote "Serpent in the Bosom," and that would be Professor Emeritus Lenard J. Cohen. Are you familiar with the length of Professor Cohen's career, where he taught, and any of his publications?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I have to say that I'm not familiar with that. This is a quite common last name and it is pronounced Cohen. It's a Jewish last name. I have a colleague and a friend with the same last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you will not dispute that Professor Cohen is co-founder of the school for international studies at Simon Fraser University. Has been Professor emeritus since 2009, has been in the field for over 35 years and has numerous publications including at least two well-received books?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Of course I do not dispute that, but does it not seem usual to you that someone who is writing a report about circumstances in the territory of the former Yugoslavia should study all the constitutional documents, if not all the laws? Therefore, it was only logical that Professor Donia who has a good mastery of the Serbian language - I'm not sure about Cohen - should study the amendments of the constitution and then conclude or draw his conclusion on the basis of that as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At page 19 of your report, and there the operative -- this is a -- the section -- section 3 of that part of your report beginning: Hiding and withholding relevant facts, and it's a portion that refers to page 9 of Dr. Donia's report: "Bosnian Serb Leadership and the Siege of Sarajevo." And it addresses or responds to a portion of Dr. Donia's report stating: "According to the 1991 census, these municipalities held relatively high percentages of Yugoslavs: 16.4 per cent in Centar, 15.9 per cent in Novo Sarajevo, and 11.4 per cent in Novi Grad." And the discussion and the critique that you provide there is about his alleged failure to adduce the real reasons why people declared themselves as Yugoslavs and your assertion that Serbs are Yugoslavs and no Croats and Slovenes are Yugoslavs. And in that connection I just wanted to ask you one question, and that was: Do you -- is it true that as back in -- during the war 1994 and around that operative time that the Muslims tended to consider Yugoslavs as Muslims, the Croats considered the Yugoslavs as Croats, and as you've indicated the Serbs considered Yugoslavs as Serbs? Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I didn't understand you fully. Do you mean that I said that Muslims were Muslims, Croats were Croats, and many Serbs declared themselves as Yugoslavs? Is that what you're alleging?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. First I drew your attention to the portion of your report and what your position was in that connection, and then I asked you more generally whether you considered it accurate to assert that Muslims tended to consider Yugoslavs as Muslims and Croats considered the Yugoslavs as Croats, and of course you've already indicated your position that you considered the Serbs -- Yugoslavs as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Unfortunately your question is not well phrased. Talking about citizenship, all the citizens of Yugoslavia were Yugoslavs because they had the Yugoslav citizenship but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I hope it was clear from context that I'm talking about how people self-described, how people declared themselves in the census. And you address in that portion of your report your position that those people who declared themselves Yugoslavs were Serbs, and I'm asking you if it wasn't the case that Muslims tended to consider Yugoslavs as those people as Muslims and Croats tended to think that they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: God forbid, a Muslim, Ejup Ganic, declared himself a Yugoslav to win the elections to the Presidency, and then it turned out not only that he was an ordinary participant but a very active participant in everything that happened during the war. He was a member of the Crisis Staff. There is a suspicion that he ordered the attack on the convoy of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor -- I mean, Professor, I don't think that that can fairly be described as an attempt to answer my question rather than an attempt to talk about something you've already addressed repeatedly in your report. If you can't answer my question, that's fine; if you can, please do so. I've asked it twice, I think it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. You don't really know the situations in the former Yugoslavia. I can tell you openly that the Slovenians have always been Slovenians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Cavoski, I'm sorry to interrupt. Whether Mr. Tieger knows or not, you can answer yes or no, and you can explain it. Could you concentrate on answering the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my mind, the Yugoslavs for the most part were Serbs and there were also some people from mixed marriages who also declared themselves as Yugoslavs. This is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite an answer because I asked you -- I appreciate the fact that that's what's in your mind, but I asked you if in the minds of Muslims the Yugoslavs were Muslims and in the minds of Croats they were Croats. That was my question. And as I said if you can't answer that, that's --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: No. To be frank, I don't know. But I'm almost certain that both the Croats and the Muslims knew that those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs were almost, without exception, Serbs. They knew that because I know the situation there unlike you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I asked you that question because we've received evidence that that's exactly what Dr. Karadzic said in 1994 to the members of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And that's found at P1385, English page 114, and B/C/S page 84 through 85. Let me move on to a different topic, something that you raised during the course of your direct examination. And that was your explanation that -- about your role in constituting the committee on establishing the truth on Dr. Karadzic. Now, that -- and if I could call up 65 ter 24933. That article from "Glas Javnosti" concerns the founding in mid-November of 2001 of the international board for truth about Radovan Karadzic, describing who some of the members were, and so on. That's a reflection of the same board or committee you were talking about in your examination-in-chief; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there are various descriptions of the purpose of the board and the positions of various participants in the board concerning Dr. Karadzic. You're quoted as stating that Dr. Karadzic is the herald of Serbian freedom, the creator of Republika Srpska, the chivalrous knight who will not surrender. And did that -- does that accurately capture your position at the time concerning Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, most probably. I don't really remember the details but I think that this is most probably what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6289, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to your work on behalf of the board for truth or committee for truth about Radovan Karadzic, you also worked as a member of the Defence team as a volunteer, that is, you were not paid for that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could call up 65 ter 40614A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. This is a video -- that's a transcript of a video of a television show on Kopernikus television. You can turn to the video any time you want, but we have the transcript provided as well. And we can see in a portion of that transcript where you confirm your work on the Defence team. And that's a -- that's the portion that would be in the video from 48.46 to 49.53. I'm happy to play that video for you, sir, if it's easier.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I can see it all. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to -- I won't leave this video just yet because I wanted to ask you about something else you said during the course of your testimony, and that is your references to what you called analyses of the work of the Tribunal. And on this show as well, you spoke out about aspects of the work of the Tribunal, in particular the payment to Defence lawyers and your position on what that meant, what its purpose and effects were, and did so specifically in the context of lawyer Vujin. Do you recall that or would you like to see the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the -- let's bear in mind, of course, that the accused led evidence about this witness's analyses and publications concerning the Tribunal, presumably an attempt to bolster his credibility. At a minimum I'm certainly entitled to address what it is he is actually saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think, you know, we're mixing things here. First of all, certainly the fact that he was working for free for the Defence team is very relevant, on this first page that has been shown to the witness is definitely relevant. But his complaints about payment to the Defence team, operation of this trial, don't seem to be relevant to either his credibility or any of the issues in the indictment and that's what I'm objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, to the extent -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it should be clear that to the extent those representations are inaccurate are, in fact, misrepresentations. It's very relevant to this witness's credibility, especially in the context in which this was raised. I'm not surprised Mr. Robinson is trying to avoid further scrutiny of this, but it's a highly relevant issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just reply one second. You know, at the time these statements were made, the president has reversed the Registrar four times on the funding of the Defence team so we're getting into a lot of collateral issues. So if Dr. Cavoski or Professor Cavoski at one point said that the Defence team was underfunded, well the President has found that we were underfunded on four separate occasions during the course of this case. So I don't see how it affects the credibility or is relevant. And it just brings in collateral issues that so far we didn't believe were relevant to the trial or else we would have brought them up ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is not the funding -- this is not in connection with the funding of this particular Defence team's composition, so maybe that's the nature of the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger. Please, we'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor, in connection with that matter, you stated at - and this would be at e-court page 3 of this exhibit - you explained that what happened in the court was -- and used the expression: He who pays the piper calls the tune, but that there are some lawyers who overstepped the boundaries which were tacitly placed, claimed that that's what happened to Mr. Vujin who was cruelly punished for overstepping these attempted boundaries, as you say, above people who would bring these proceedings into question too much. And use that as an example of the fact that lawyers cannot properly work at the Tribunal. So you took the position publicly that the payment of remuneration to lawyers was a way of controlling them so they couldn't properly represent their client and that anyone who overstepped those boundaries was cruelly punished so -- as a threat and to bully other lawyers into compliance. That's what you were telling the public when you made this interview; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I don't understand the relevance of this at all. This -- how this goes to the witness's credibility or that it's anything relevant. If someone is critical of this institution -- for example, if someone is critical of the jury system in the United States or in the United Kingdom, does the jury get to hear that as something that's reflecting on their credibility? So I don't see where -- this is just an effort to try to show the Chamber that someone is before them who disagrees with this institution, and I don't think that should be relevant to your assessment of Professor Cavoski's credibility and I don't think it's relevant to anything that's an issue of substance in Dr. Karadzic's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's cut to the chase, Mr. President, if I may, on this. I have not and had no intention of eliciting this witness's many criticisms of the Tribunal, no matter -- for the most part, no matter how outlandish I considered them to be, but this is a different matter. This is a matter of misrepresenting a particular state of events and then I might as well be clear about it now, the fact of the matter is that Mr. Vujin was convicted for putting forward false statements, manipulating witnesses, to the detriment of his client. So my position is that Professor Cavoski in doing this is publicly making misrepresentations for a particular purpose, and that particular purpose does reflect on his credibility. And that particular circumstance reflects on his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Chamber sees no reason to change its position. Do you remember the question, Mr. Cavoski, or shall I ask Mr. Tieger to repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the question. This is not the first time somebody has tried to make an issue of my critical attitude towards this Court. I have published articles about this and that is available to the Prosecutor. As for this Tribunal, I have from the very beginning considered that there was no equality of arms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. No, it's not related to general criticism about this Tribunal. I will ask Mr. Tieger to put his question specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, first of all, I just wanted as a preliminary step to confirm that this is what you said about both the practice -- okay. So this accurately reflects what you stated. Okay. It's also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's hear the witness. Please wait a minute until the interpretation is over. Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's also the fact, is it not, Professor Cavoski, that Mr. Vujin was sanctioned and not for overstepping boundaries that would -- about being too aggressive on behalf of his client, but instead for putting forward false statements, manipulating witnesses, of all against his own client's interest. In other words, he was convicted of contempt and that's why he was sanctioned, precisely the opposite of what you were representing in the Kopernikus interview?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I can give a very clear answer. I said that and I said it based on what Mr. Vujin had related to me. I co-operated with him when I was to participate on the Defence of Stanislav Galic. What I said is based on his words and I've never seen the Court's decision. I know very well how Dusko Tadic fared who was an insignificant reserve police officer. Nowadays he wouldn't be at this Tribunal at all, but he was in the early days. And about these lawyers, I spoke to many one of them and I was able to be convinced when I went to the office of Mr. Vujin. During the trial, his colleague Ms. Pilipovic appeared as the Defence counsel because Mr. Vujin wasn't allowed to. And he hired me to write a report. Here's what I noticed. He gave me a text, about 300 pages long, and it was the report of one James Gow, a historian, who at the time appeared in the same role as Donia did. But he started his report with historical situation from Emperor Dusan's times and the Kosovo battle. The Court wanted to make that an adjudicated fact and incorporate that into the Galic judgement. But I criticised him harshly and said that not only didn't he know history, but he was also malevolus. I also engaged Rados Ljusic, who was an excellent professor of history at the faculty of philosophy, and Ms. Stefanovski, my colleague, who teaches the history of law. And with their assistance I wrote a report. I asked him to have it translated into English and show it to the Court. When I asked him what he had sent, it turned out that it wasn't a translation of what I had written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Professor -- Professor --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: So he didn't dare or wasn't allowed to send what I had written. Later on I published that as a book in Serbian, the title is: "The Judging of History in The Hague." James Gow was not hired anymore nor did any historian deal with events before the year 1980 after this criticism of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Whether or not that's a very clear answer to my question, I leave to the Court but I will move on in the interests of time. I wanted to ask you a bit more about your work on the committee --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender the last exhibit, Mr. President, which was 65 ter 40614A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have any objection to pages 1 and 3, that's what were shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in connection with your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You're not tendering the videotape itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I would tender the videotape as well [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you object to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The parts that were not put to the witness shouldn't be admitted, yes. It's been our practice only to admit those portions of things -- he can't scroll like we can, he's only been asked and commented on pages 1 and 3, so that's all that should be admitted. But if Mr. Tieger wants to go through the other two, we would agree they can be admitted after the witness had a chance to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Admitting page 1 and 3 won't hurt the flow of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's been the case with documents as short as this, four pages, but I'm not going to quibble at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask you further about your work on the committee, sir, and in that regard because you -- if I understood you correctly, you stated that you assembled documents that were signed, orders that were issued, interviews, et cetera, et cetera. So you collected and then reproduced various documents. Now, in connection with the assembly of those documents and the acquisition of those documents, were you in contact with Mr. Karadzic for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely, but I believe it was either in late 1986 [as interpreted] or 1987 [as interpreted] when Dr. Karadzic simply disappeared. It wasn't possible to set up contact with him. But I contacted his brother and his cousin. From his brother, Luka Karadzic, who lives in Belgrade I received these documents and his daughter, Radmila, a very nice and well-educated girl, entered that into a computer. I read the printed texts and revised them and proofread them. I also gave some texts in Serbian to translators to have them translated into English. And to the extent that I know English - and my knowledge isn't perfect - I tried to see if it's well translated and understandable. Most of these texts were received from Luka Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I want to show you another document and ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if we could call up 65 ter 24910A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a letter dated the 1st of October, 2001, from Dr. Karadzic to Miroslav Toholj that appears in Toholj's book: "Night Post Correspondence with Radovan Karadzic," which was published after Mr. Karadzic's arrest and it covers letters from 1996 to 2004. And if we could turn to page 2 of the English and page 2 of the Serbian, Dr. Karadzic writes: "I'm glad that the material for the site is slowly building up and that the number of pages is growing. I also wrote to Kosta and I'm very grateful to him for accepting the work in the committee and for his commenting on the orders. I believe that he could also review the other enclosures and that he can comment on them." On page 3 of the English, and I believe still on page 3 of the Serbian, there is another reference: "I believe that you in the editor's office (although I believe that it is you and Kosta as Jovan is in Herceg Novi) will assess it appropriately, maybe even group it differently, as Ljiljana did it in a more or less chronological order ..." And at the next page in English and I believe the next page in Serbian we see the following reference about publishing poems for children: "There might possibly be some space for these poems also in the 'Christian thought' which I frequently receive from Kosta." Now, those are references to you, sir; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we return to page 2 of the English and also page 2 of the Serbian, we can find a further description of the enclosures that were referenced or that were referred to in the previous references. And there we see the following: "I am sending you these disks that Ljiljana gathered. On the ones I'm sending you, I deleted all that I thought should not go (I saved the originals) but there might be more reductions necessary. I trust that you will review each report and make a decision on it yourself." And then it continues some lines later after references to interviews and speeches from Assemblies and so on: "Of course, I did not mention our worst disgraces, but I do think that some of the things that disgrace us, up to an acceptable level, should be published. I was particularly careful of not jeopardising anyone. I also got rid of everything that would jeopardise anyone or that would look like a non-gentlemanly stone-throwing at Slobodan or his prime minister." But he also notes that open letters to him, and so on, have already been published so there's nothing to hide and then it continues with the reference that I noted earlier, that those of you in the editor's office, including you and Kosta will assess it appropriately and maybe even group it differently. Now, this, in fact, is a reflection of Dr. Karadzic's role in providing materials for publication that were deemed acceptable and that eliminated those items that he considered should not be published; correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA CAVOSKI
utterances.text: I must say that I have no idea what Miroslav Toholj's role was in all of this was. I received the documents, as I said, mostly from Luka Karadzic and together with Radmilo -- Radmila, the daughter of Radovan Karadzic, I edited all of that. I think there were a couple of friends of Dr. Karadzic who are excellent authors and know the language well to help me to edit things because my knowledge is not so great in the sphere of language. So they helped me to do the best possible job. So Karadzic did not provide me with those documents. I don't know how they reached me. I had photocopies of documents with the proper heading and signature, and I entered those documents into six collected volumes of his political acts. I had photocopies. I did not receive any diskettes. What I know was on diskette that I later saw at the book fair was the book which was later transcribed by Toholj. I know that he frequently wrote letters during the period of his hiding. I received some of those letters, but this was such a long time ago or there were such long intervals in between, so that when I gave the letters to his daughter to somehow get them to him I would receive the replies even a year later.
